chunks: PFM versus PWM in buck converters. The question: What is the difference between PFM and PWM?
PWM and PFM are two ways to regulate. In PWM the switching frequency is fixed and the pulse width changes with load.
In PFM every pulse is the same size and the controller changes how often it fires. PWM is quiet and fast, but wasteful at light load. PFM is efficient at light load, but noisier.
Think of two bus services. PWM runs buses on a fixed timetable, every few minutes, and resizes the bus to match the crowd.
PFM uses one bus size and runs it more or less often depending on the crowd. A bus that starts its engine costs fuel each time.
With a fixed timetable you pay the start-up cost constantly, even when almost nobody rides.
The analogy hides the noise side: PFM's irregular timing makes the output noise harder to filter.
High-side gate drive. PWM (blue) always repeats at the same period and changes the width: wide at heavy load, narrow at light load, but never fewer pulses.
PFM (green) keeps each pulse the same width and stretches the gaps as the load falls. (Schematic only; real timing has different scales.)
PWM: a fixed frequency with a changing duty cycle ("Buck operating modes (CCM, DCM, PFM)"). PFM: fixed-size pulses with a changing rate ("Explain PFM operation in a buck").
Light-load efficiency: efficiency at small output currents, where fixed losses dominate. EMI: unwanted electrical noise; noise spread over many frequencies is harder to filter.
Forced-PWM: a mode pin that keeps the converter in PWM even at light load.
Suppose each switching cycle costs 1 µJ of gate drive and switch losses. In PWM at 500 kilohertz that is 1 micro J times 500 k equals 0.
5 watts, even if the load needs almost nothing. In PFM at a light load that needs only 2,000 pulses per second, it is 1 micro J times 2000 equals 2 milliwatts.
That is the whole idea.
"PWM keeps the frequency fixed and varies the pulse width; PFM keeps the pulse size fixed and varies how often it fires.
PWM gives a clean fixed-frequency spectrum, low ripple and fast response, but poor light-load efficiency because it switches constantly.
PFM scales switching losses with load so it's efficient at light load, but has larger low-frequency ripple, smeared EMI and a slower response to load steps.
ICs combine both automatically."
